name: Aer
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Shafqat, Asmara; Javeria Ali Wadho; Nida Shabbir. 2025. Voices from the periphery: a constraint-based analysis of phonological variation in Sindhi's Aer and Bhaya endangered languages. Contemporary Journal of Social Science Review 3(3): 2353-2367. Open PDF:https://contemporaryjournal.com/index.php/14/article/download/1259/1086(DOI 10.63878/cjssr.v3i3.1259).
catalog_locator: Abstract p. 2353; sect. 4.3.1 'Stress Patterns' pp. 2362-2363; also lit review p. 2357 ('the Aer variation of Sindhi, which likewise has a fixed beginning stress'; paragraph repeated on p. 2358) and discussion sect. 5.2 pp. 2364-2365
catalog_quote: [Abstract, p. 2353] Prosodic features also differ; Aer exhibits fixed initial stress, whereas Bhaya allows for variable stress placement depending on the morphological structure. [Sect. 4.3.1 'Stress Patterns', pp. 2362-2363] The most notable variation in patterns of stress between Aer and Bhaya is the positioning of stress. Aer has a consistent beginning stress pattern, with the initially stressed syllable on an expression or word receiving the predominant emphasis. In contrast, Bhaya has a variable stress position, which can change depending on the morphological foundation or sentence focus. Example: • Aer: "important"—/ˈɪm.pɔː.tənt/ (fixed initial stress) • Bhaya: "important" – /ɪmˈpɔː.tənt/ (variable stress placement) The stress on the initial syllable in Aer is predictable and unchanging, but in Bhaya, stress can shift to the subsequent syllable, especially in words with multiple sounds or lengthy morphological constructions. The Praat study of the pitch curves discovered that for Aer, the pitch's peak was on the first syllable, which supported the consistent stress pattern. [Sect. 5.2, p. 2365] In comparison, Aer had an increasingly equal patterning, with similar preference for the first syllable of each word, which is compatible with previous studies on fixed stress patterns across languages for example Hindi (Bharati, 2007).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked. The quoted passage is at sect. 4.3.1 'Stress Patterns', p. 2362 (the text) exactly as given, with the [..] ellipses covering the English-word 'example' bullets and one clause; the abstract (p. 2353) sentence 'Aer exhibits fixed initial stress, whereas Bhaya allows for variable stress placement depending on the morphological structure' is also verbatim, and the claim recurs in the lit review (p. 2356 'Aer.. likewise has a fixed beginning stress') and discussion 5.2 (p. 2364-5 'Aer's initial stress.. system', 'preference for the first syllable of each word'). So as a reading of what the source asserts, fixed: initial syllable is correct and internally consistent across the paper…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word in Aer, predictably and without alternation (authors' fieldwork claim, supported only by pitch-peak observation; contrasted with variable stress in Bhaya).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only 'example' given is the English word 'important' transcribed /ˈɪm.pɔː.tənt/, not an Aer word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('an expression or word'); based on word lists, picture naming and narratives from 20 speakers, Praat pitch contours; no citation-form vs phrase distinction made.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2025 article calls Aer (and Bhaya) 'lesser-documented varieties/dialects of the Sindhi language' spoken in 'remote towns of southeastern/southern Sindh'; it gives no ISO code, village names or classification. Ethnologue/Glottolog Aer [aeq, aerr1238] is a Gujarati-related (Western Gujaratic, close to Kachi Koli) language of Jhikrio Goth (Deh 333 near Hyderabad) and Jamesabad (Kunri area), i.e. lower/southeastern Sindh, and Bhaya [bhe] is likewise an Ethnologue-listed micro-language of lower Sindh, so the referent is very probably the same community, but the match is inferred, not stated. The paper's quality is poor (English-word 'example', internal contradictions, unverifiable references), so the statement should enter the catalog flagged low-confidence.

Illustrated only with the English word 'important'; low-quality paper (Aer treated as a 'dialect of Sindhi', no sites/ISO codes, abstract contradicts body on retroflexes, several references look unverifiable).
